situation.text: You and a friend are at a stadium. You invite him to a game on Saturday and plan what to do before it starts.

pages.title: Cultural snapshot — Sports in the USA
pages.intro: Sports are a big part of weekends in the USA. Fans meet, eat and talk before the game even starts. Look and guess before you read.

cards.pt: Festa no estacionamento antes do jogo
cards.note: Fans cook and eat in the parking lot before a game. This is called tailgating.
In the USA, “football” means American football. Our “futebol” is called “soccer”.
Hot dogs, burgers and snacks are common at games.

levels.A2: Fans eat and talk in the parking lot before the game.
levels.B1: Tailgating is a social tradition: people grill food and hang out near their cars before a game.
levels.B2: Tailgating turns the game into a community event: the food and the company are part of the day.

qs.q: What is the difference between “soccer” and “football” in the USA?
qs.pt: Qual a diferença entre “soccer” e “football” nos EUA?

levels.A2: Soccer is our “futebol”. Football is a different sport.
levels.B1: American “football” is played with an oval ball and a lot of tackling, so the other sport is called “soccer”.
levels.B2: The word “football” belongs to a different sport in the USA, so Americans use “soccer” for the game the rest of the world calls football.

qs.q: How do people show they are fans?
qs.pt: Como as pessoas mostram que são torcedoras?

levels.A2: They wear team colors and say “Go, team!”.
levels.B1: Fans wear jerseys and caps and cheer with the crowd.
levels.B2: Wearing team colors is a way of belonging; strangers often start conversations about the team.

pages.compare: In Brazil people also talk a lot about their team and often watch the game with friends. What do you usually do before a game?

teach.goal: Ativar o contexto cultural e as primeiras hipóteses.
solo: Mostre os 3 cartões e peça hipóteses antes de explicar.
Peça que o estudante compare com o que acontece no Brasil.
group: Cada estudante escolhe um cartão e explica em uma frase.
Pergunte “Do you agree?” entre colegas.
answers: Q1: festa e comida no estacionamento antes do jogo.
Q2: soccer = nosso futebol; football = futebol americano.
Q3: camisa do time e “Go, team!”.
extra: What do you eat during a game?
What is a perfect Saturday for you?
support: Use as respostas do nível A1 como andaime e peça que repitam.
stretch: B2: compare as convenções sociais do Brasil e dos EUA nessa situação.

pages.title: Pronunciation lab — natural American English
pages.tip: In fast speech, “want to” often sounds like “wanna” and “let us” becomes “let’s”. You do not need to say “wanna” — but you should understand it.

items.say: What are you doing on Saturday?

own.prompt: Write a question with “Do you want to…?” about a plan you really have.
own.criteria: Say it slowly, then fast with “wanna”. Can your partner understand both?

solo: 3 passagens: escutar e identificar → reproduzir ritmo e entonação → usar em frase com conteúdo próprio.
Modele devagar e normal; peça que o estudante bata palmas na sílaba forte.
group: Coro, depois duplas; circule ouvindo.
Cada estudante cria uma frase própria.
answers: Identify: Do you want to play? · Let’s go to the game.

pages.title: Personalized roleplay — plan a game day

brief.teacher: You are a friend who loves sports (change the plan during the scene!).
brief.student: You are the friend: invite, choose a team and organize the day.

orders: Invite a friend to a soccer game
Invite a friend to play basketball in the park
Invite a friend to watch the game at home
complications: Your friend is busy on that day: suggest another day.
Your friend supports the other team: joke about it kindly.
Your friend asks what to bring: answer.
The place is far: agree where to meet.

pages.title: Writing — a small real-life task
pages.task: Write a short text message to invite a friend to a game this weekend.
pages.model: Hi Jonas! **Do you want to** watch the game on Saturday? **Let’s meet** at noon at the stadium. **I’ll bring** the snacks. **Go, Tigers!**
checklist: I invited him with “Do you want to…?”.
I gave a time and a place.
I closed with a friendly phrase.
pages.tip: Fix only 2–3 priority points. Show a more natural way to say the same idea instead of rewriting everything.

criteria.name: Language use

interpret.text: Needs more support. Revisit the main patterns with guided practice before the next lesson.
Functional performance. Work on the lowest criteria in the next lesson.

Strong performance. Move to a more demanding situation.

pages.title: Level up — the same situation from A1 to C2
pages.intro: You do not need six different methods: the structure stays, while language complexity and autonomy grow.

ladder.goal: Accept a plan with short phrases.

ladder.say: Do you want to play soccer on Saturday? Let’s meet at ten.
I was thinking of watching the game at my place. Would you be up for it?
If you’re free on Saturday, we could catch the game together and grab something after.
I wouldn’t mind catching the game on Saturday, if you happen to be around.
It would be a shame to let the weekend slip by without us seeing that match.

pages.note: This progression is illustrative: complex sentences do not define a level on their own. CEFR also considers comprehension, autonomy, fluency, accuracy, interaction and appropriateness.
